# Written, published law code (`written_law_code`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: needs writing_invention; helped by rule_of_law
- Core idea: Rules and penalties are written down, displayed in public and applied to cases as written, instead of living in the memory of elders or the will of a judge. This makes outcomes predictable, limits arbitrary judgment and lets a subject know in advance what is forbidden and what a contract or injury will cost. A code that works needs little: cases stated as "if X, then Y", a public copy in the language people speak, judges who must cite it, and a way to amend it. Fixed fines and compensation in place of blood feud are the usual first gain.
- Pitfalls:
  - Assuming Hammurabi's was the first code: Ur-Namma's is about 350 years older, and Lipit-Ishtar and Eshnunna also precede it
  - Assuming Mesopotamian 'codes' were statutes that courts applied: surviving court records almost never cite them, and many scholars read them as royal self-praise or scribal case collections
  - Thinking written law is automatically just or equal: most early codes set different penalties by rank (free, commoner, slave)
  - Publishing a code nobody can read or that the ruler may ignore: writing limits judges, it does not by itself bind the king
  - Believing 'an eye for an eye' was a call to cruelty: it capped revenge, and for lower ranks the same codes used money payments
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2350 BC – Urukagina of Lagash records reforms (no code survives); c. 2100 BC Code of Ur-Namma, the oldest surviving, mostly money compensation; c. 1930 BC Lipit-Ishtar; c. 1770 BC Eshnunna; c. 1754 BC Hammurabi, 282 provisions on a public stele; egypt: no law code survives from the pharaonic period, though written laws are mentioned; a Demotic legal manual from Hermopolis dates to the 3rd c. BC; india: 3rd c. BC – Ashoka publishes royal instructions and moral exhortations on rocks and pillars; dharma texts (Dharmasutras, later Manu, c. 2nd c. BC–2nd c. AD) are learned treatises rather than enacted codes; china: 536 BC – Zichan of Zheng has penal laws cast on bronze vessels, criticised at the time for making people argue from the text; 217 BC Qin statutes on the Shuihudi bamboo slips; 653 Tang Code with commentary, the model for East Asia; east_asia: 701 – Taiho Code in Japan, modelled on Tang law; Korea and Vietnam adopt Tang-style codes; greece: c. 650 BC – inscribed law at Dreros (Crete), the oldest Greek law on stone; 621/620 BC Draco at Athens; 594 BC Solon; c. 450 BC Gortyn code; rome: 451–450 BC – Twelve Tables set up in the Forum; AD 529–534 Justinian's Corpus Iuris Civilis; islamic: 8th–9th c. – law developed by jurists (fiqh) rather than enacted; 15th–16th c. Ottoman kanun codes (Mehmed II, Suleiman); 1869–1876 Mecelle civil code; europe: c. 500 – Germanic codes (Lex Salica); 1804 Napoleon's Code civil, the model of modern codification
- Read:
  - Martha T. Roth, Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor (1995)
  - Raymond Westbrook (ed.), A History of Ancient Near Eastern Law (2003)
